<design_philosophy>
You are building ONE web page whose only job is to let a reader understand a research paper faster
than they could by opening the PDF. Every decision on the page is judged against that.

WHAT "FASTER" MEANS HERE
- A reader who leaves after thirty seconds still knows the finding and the number behind it.
- A reader who stays five minutes has the method, the figures and the caveats, in that order.
- Nothing on the page is there because a layout had a slot for it.

ACCURACY IS THE HARD CONSTRAINT
Every number, name and claim comes from the paper as written — you read them out of the LaTeX
source, the only source this page has. You never change a number's precision, never restate a
comparison the paper did not make, and never invent a headline figure to fill a card. A page that
looks excellent and misreports one result is worse than no page, because the PDF beside it says
something else and a reader will find that out.

CRAFT, AND THE LOOK TO AVOID
The failure mode for a generated page is a look every reader now recognises on sight: a
purple-to-blue gradient banner, three identical cards with emoji headings, and body text set in
one weight at one size. Avoid all of it.
- Type carries the design. One system font stack, a real scale with visible jumps between levels
  rather than a creep of similar sizes, long-form text around 17-19px with a measure of 65-75
  characters and generous line height. Weight and size do the emphasis; colour rarely does.
- Colour is restrained. A light, near-white ground, one dark ink for text, one accent used for
  links and the current-section marker and almost nothing else. No gradients as decoration.
- Space does the work that borders and boxes would do badly. Sections separated by real vertical
  rhythm, cards defined by alignment and a single hairline rather than by shadow stacks.
- Structure over ornament: no emoji as section markers, no icon fonts, no badge clutter, no
  animated counters.
- Motion is a courtesy. A short transition on a lightbox or a hover state is welcome; anything
  that moves on scroll, autoplays, or delays the reader is not — and all of it stops under
  prefers-reduced-motion.
- Every interactive element works with a keyboard and says what it is to a screen reader. That is
  part of the craft, not a checklist bolted on at the end.

FINISH IT
The page is done when you have opened it in a browser, read it at a phone width and a desktop
width, tabbed through every control, and found nothing to fix. Not before.
</design_philosophy>

<page_structure>
In this order, top to bottom:

1. HERO — the paper's title, the author line as the paper gives it, and a one-paragraph TL;DR in
   plain language: what was asked, what was found, and the single number that carries the finding.
   Not the abstract, and not a rewrite of it. Below it, every link the links section below
   lists, each at the exact URL given there.
2. CONTRIBUTIONS — the paper's actual contributions as three to five scannable cards, each a short
   heading plus one or two sentences. If the paper claims four things, show four cards, not five.
3. METHOD — a walkthrough a technically literate non-specialist can follow: what goes in, what
   happens to it, what comes out, and why the design is the way it is. Lead with the paper's own
   method figure when it has one.
4. RESULTS — the paper's real headline numbers, read out of `paper.tex`, each next to what it was measured on and what it is being compared against.
   A number that is not in the paper does not go on the page, and neither does a comparison the
   paper did not make. If a slot has no number, drop the slot.
5. FIGURE GALLERY — every figure, each with its caption, click-to-enlarge into a lightbox that
   closes on Escape, on a click outside, and on a visible close control.
6. LIMITATIONS — what the paper says it does not show. Verbatim in substance; do not soften it.
7. FOOTER — every link from the links section again, and the citation if the paper carries one.

A sticky section navigation runs alongside all of it and marks where the reader currently is.
Do NOT write its highlighting yourself: hand-written ones kept a stale section lit after a jump
back to the top, or never reached the short last sections. Instead give the nav element a
`data-scrollspy` attribute, make each of its links `href="#<id of that section>"`, style the
current link through `a.active` (it also gets `aria-current`), and paste this script VERBATIM
into the page's script element at the end of the body. It lights the section in view, the last one once the page is
scrolled to its end, and nothing while the reader is above the first linked section:

```js
/* aii-scroll-spy v1: paste verbatim */
(function () {
  var links = [], targets = [];
  document.querySelectorAll('[data-scrollspy] a[href^="#"]').forEach(function (a) {
    var el = document.getElementById(a.getAttribute('href').slice(1));
    if (el) { links.push(a); targets.push(el); }
  });
  if (!links.length) return;
  var queued = false;
  function current() {
    var view = window.innerHeight;
    var doc = document.documentElement;
    var atEnd = window.scrollY > 0 && view + window.scrollY >= doc.scrollHeight - 2;
    var line = atEnd ? view - 1 : Math.min(view * 0.3, 200);
    var best = null, bestTop = -Infinity;
    targets.forEach(function (el) {
      var top = el.getBoundingClientRect().top;
      if (top <= line && top > bestTop) { best = el; bestTop = top; }
    });
    return best;
  }
  function update() {
    queued = false;
    var el = current();
    links.forEach(function (a, i) {
      var on = targets[i] === el;
      a.classList.toggle('active', on);
      if (on) a.setAttribute('aria-current', 'location');
      else a.removeAttribute('aria-current');
    });
  }
  function schedule() {
    if (!queued) { queued = true; window.requestAnimationFrame(update); }
  }
  window.addEventListener('scroll', schedule, { passive: true });
  window.addEventListener('resize', schedule);
  window.addEventListener('load', schedule);
  if (window.ResizeObserver) new ResizeObserver(schedule).observe(document.body);
  update();
})();
```
</page_structure>

<technical_requirements>
- ONE file. All CSS in a style element, all JavaScript in a script element, both inline in
  `index.html`. No build step, no bundler, no framework, no external script, stylesheet, web
  font or analytics — nothing fetched at load time. The page must render with the network off,
  and the only local files it may point at are the figures listed above; the PDF is linked at
  its full URL, never by its local name.
- A complete HTML document: the file opens with exactly this markup, then the title and the
  style element, and closes head before the body. The viewport tag is what makes a phone lay the
  page out at its own width; without it the page renders 980px wide and shrinks to tiny text.
```html
<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```
- System font stack only, since no font may be downloaded.
- Light theme. Responsive from a 360px phone to a wide desktop, with no horizontal page scroll;
  wide content scrolls inside its own container.
- Honour prefers-reduced-motion: under it, transitions and any scroll-driven effect stop.
- Keyboard-navigable: every control reachable by Tab in a sensible order, a visible focus ring,
  the lightbox trapping focus while open and returning it to the thumbnail on close, and a skip
  link to the main content.
- Semantic HTML: one top-level heading, headings that descend without skipping, landmark elements,
  and alt text on every image that says what the figure shows rather than repeating its number.
- No emoji anywhere. No purple-to-blue gradients. No decorative icon fonts.
- Keep the whole file comfortably under a megabyte.
</technical_requirements>

<writing_register>
Write in the register of the field's best papers (the paper this page presents, which was written to them), not in the register of a language
model. Four things are measured on the finished draft, and a draft outside them is sent back with
the numbers:
- Never use: delve, underscore, showcase, intricate, pivotal, realm, commendable, meticulous, tapestry, garner, multifaceted, it is worth noting, plays a crucial role, not only ... but also. These are 10 to 30 times more frequent in machine-written abstracts than in
  human ones, and reviewers read them as such.
- Em dashes: at most 3 per 1,000 words. Use a comma, a colon or a full stop.
- Sentence rhythm: mix short and long sentences. An interquartile range of sentence length under
  8 words reads as machine-written.
- Hedging: at most 15 hedges (may, likely, suggests, appears) per 1,000
  words. State what the evidence supports plainly; hedge where it is thin, not everywhere.
Style never changes substance: numbers, claims, citations and figure markers stay exactly as the
evidence gives them. The user's original request (delivered as a separate message) overrides all
of this wherever the two conflict.
</writing_register>

Two programs can differ in every line and implement the same algorithm, and a program can name one algorithm while executing another, so labels must come from what the code does when run. Comparisons across temperatures drawn with independent random numbers mix the effect of temperature with sampling noise; with a default share near 1.0, a few stray samples look like a temperature effect. This design ran on one 8-bit engine only -- bf16 does not fit the 16 GB GPU used -- and was not rerun in bf16.}\n  \\label{fig:headline}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\section{Related Work}\n\\label{sec:related}\n\n\\paragraph{Diversity collapse and creativity in code models.} Alignment narrows output diversity relative to the variety available for a task~\\citep{Wu2024,Kirk2023}, reduces conceptual diversity~\\citep{Murthy2025}, and leaves base models better at randomness and creative generation than their aligned descendants~\\citep{West2025}. The structure of the chat format alone contributes to this collapse~\\citep{Yun2025}. The typicality bias learned from human preferences has been linked to mode collapse that verbalized sampling partly undoes~\\citep{Zhang2025a}. In code, \\citet{Lee2025} find that models concentrate on few algorithms among correct solutions, and \\citet{Narula2026} show that subtle prompt cues steer which algorithm is chosen. Denial prompting, which forbids the technique of the previous solution, is used to measure creativity in code generation~\\citep{Lu2025}. Benchmarks of humanlike diversity~\\citep{Zhang2025} and the distinction between approach-level and surface-level diversity in mathematical reasoning~\\citep{Lee2026} motivate counting ideas separately from phrasings. We adopt that separation for code, with ideas defined by runtime behaviour, and we measure it under coupled randomness so that the effect of a control on a single sample can be read directly.\n\n\\paragraph{Temperature and decoding.} Truncation samplers such as nucleus sampling~\\citep{Holtzman2019} and min-p sampling~\\citep{Nguyen2024} shape the token distribution at each step, and adaptive schemes raise temperature only where the next token is hard to predict~\\citep{Zhu2024,Zhang2024}. \\citet{Peeperkorn2024} find that temperature correlates only weakly with novelty in story generation. In code, \\citet{Lee2025} report that temperature above 1 raises algorithmic diversity, and \\citet{Sohail2025} observe more distinct operations in generated sorting algorithms as temperature rises from 0.75 to 1.1. Intent factored generation and plan search diversify a sampled intent or plan before writing~\\citep{Ahmed2025,Wang2024}, random embeddings injected into the input diversify reasoning paths~\\citep{Kim2026}, and the level at which randomness enters a generation pipeline changes how diverse its outputs are~\\citep{Zhang2026}. In diffusion language models, an idealized model of fork tokens motivates tempering the choice of which position to unmask, rather than the token distribution, to keep entropy at the forks~\\citep{Olausson2026}. Coupling counterfactual generations through shared Gumbel noise~\\citep{Ravfogel2024} is the closest precedent for our common-random-numbers design. Our contribution is to explain why temperature does or does not reach the algorithm, and to predict the size of its effect from one token's logits before sampling.\n\n\\paragraph{Where an output is decided.} Forking Paths analysis resamples continuations from prefixes and finds tokens after which the outcome distribution changes abruptly~\\citep{Bigelow2024}. Thought anchors identify the reasoning sentences whose resampling matters most~\\citep{Bogdan2025}. A small set of high-entropy minority tokens carries most of the effect of reinforcement learning on reasoning~\\citep{Wang2025}. Post-training shifts concentrate at a few tokens~\\citep{Meng2026}, aligned models mostly reproduce the base model's top token at ordinary positions~\\citep{Lin2023}, and learned behaviours can be enforced in the first few response tokens~\\citep{Qi2024}. Self-improvement and post-training have been described as sharpening probability onto outputs the base model already ranks highly~\\citep{Huang2024}. We extend this line to the algorithm a program implements: we locate its forking token blind, compose a temperature law over it, and measure how far post-training moved that token relative to ordinary positions.\n\n\\paragraph{Interventions on internal states and program search.} Activation steering adds a direction to the residual stream~\\citep{Rimsky2024,Arditi2024}, distributed alignment search fits subspaces in which interchange interventions reproduce a counterfactual~\\citep{Geiger2023,Wu2023}, and such subspace edits can act through pathways the model does not use naturally~\\citep{Makelov2023}. Activation steering has also been turned into an exploration method that pushes the hidden states of concurrent generations apart, which raises the diversity of reasoning paths and of generated test cases~\\citep{Khanh2026,Zhu2026}. Representation geometry is studied with geodesic distances and Isomap~\\citep{Tenenbaum2000} and, recently, manifold steering~\\citep{Wurgaft2026}; sparse autoencoders~\\citep{Lieberum2024} and the tuned lens~\\citep{Belrose2023} read intermediate states. Program search with a language model as mutator and an automatic evaluator has found new constructions and heuristics~\\citep{RomeraParedes2023,Novikov2025,Liu2024,Ye2024}. We use activation edits as tests of where the algorithm is set rather than as a diversity method, and we audit every correct program outside each task's catalogue for novelty.\n\n\\section{Method}\n\\label{sec:method}\n\nFigure~\\ref{fig:method} summarises the method. Programs are labelled by what they do when run (Section~\\ref{sec:labels}). Ideas are counted separately from phrasings (Section~\\ref{sec:ideas}). Conditions are compared on shared random streams (Section~\\ref{sec:crn}). The token that decides the algorithm is located by prefix resampling (Section~\\ref{sec:fork}). A temperature law is composed from that token's logits (Section~\\ref{sec:law}). Activation exchanges test what sets the token (Section~\\ref{sec:probes}).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig2_v0.jpg}\n  \\caption{Schematic illustration of the account and of the measurements (not data), using one minimum spanning tree example. Left to right: a rounded `Prompt' box contains the task text `Return the total weight of a minimum spanning tree of the graph.', with the words that define the task, `minimum spanning tree of the graph.', highlighted in light blue and bracketed as `task-specification states (residual stream, blocks 12 to 23)', that is, the residual stream activations at those tokens; two downward arrows above the box, labelled `task-state exchange' and `random task-state push', denote interventions applied to these states. An arrow leads to the `shared opening (61 tokens)', shown as three representative monospace code tokens (`import heapq', `graph = [[] for \\_ in range(n)]', `\\#') followed by an ellipsis marking the rest of the shared opening. A second arrow leads to a `forking token' node, above which a thermometer icon is labelled `temperature T: softmax(logits / T)' with the note `changes the algorithm only here'. From the forking token, two branches lead to the token chips `Kr' and `Prim'; the orange bar beside each chip shows the token's probability at the fork — 0.72 for `Kr', leading to the `Kruskal' outcome box, and 0.27 for `Prim', leading to the `Prim' outcome box, with each bar's fill proportional to its value. A fan of four thin lines labelled `phrasings' beside each outcome box denotes that one algorithmic idea is written out in many surface forms. A grey band spanning the bottom states the composed law `P\\_T(A) = sum over openings w\\_T(O) x sum over forking tokens pi\\_T(t $|$ O) x P(A $|$ t)'. Blue marks the pipeline from prompt to fork (boxes, arrows, the forking-token node and chips); orange marks the two realized algorithm outcomes and their fork probabilities. The 61-token opening length and the 0.72/0.27 fork split are the only numbers in the figure, drawn from teacher-forced measurements on this example; the diagram as a whole is a schematic of the proposed mechanism, not a plotted dataset.}\n  \\label{fig:method}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{Tasks, models and algorithm labels}\n\\label{sec:labels}\n\nThe study starts from two path search tasks. In the grid task, \\code{solve(grid, start, goal)} returns a valid path on a grid with walls; its catalogue holds BFS, depth-first search (hereafter DFS), bidirectional BFS, iterative deepening DFS, A* and unit weight Dijkstra, that is, Dijkstra's algorithm with every edge weight set to one. The weighted shortest path task works on a directed graph, with a catalogue of Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford with its queue variant SPFA, bidirectional Dijkstra, Floyd-Warshall and Dial's algorithm. Each has 40 to 48 seeded hidden test cases with a time limit per case, and reference implementations of every catalogue algorithm that pass all tests.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-1/experiment-1}} A further 13 tasks, the \\emph{bench} below, were derived from LeetCode problems with frozen wording and catalogues of 3 to 6 algorithms each, 684 hidden test cases in total, and references for all 54 catalogue algorithms.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-2/experiment-11}} The tasks used below are $k$-th smallest element (default: full sort), connected components (default: union find), minimum spanning tree weight (Kruskal or Prim), trapped rain water (prefix and suffix maxima or two pointers) and valid anagram (sort and compare or counting), plus substring search and first and last position in a sorted array for Gemma. A \\emph{unit} is a task paired with one model. We call a unit a \\emph{default task} when the instruct model writes one algorithm in essentially all samples, and a \\emph{mixed unit} when its unperturbed samples already contain a second algorithm at a share of roughly 0.1 to 0.4.\n\nThe main model is Qwen3-8B~\\citep{Yang2025} in non-thinking mode unless stated, with Qwen3-8B-Base for the post-training comparison. On the bench tasks, agreement between the runtime and AST labellers reached Cohen's $\\kappa$ 0.84 to 1.00, with every reference correctly labelled. On the path tasks the combined label agreed with the adjudicated gold label at $\\kappa = 0.966$ with 22 of 22 references correct, although the stricter criterion of that gate, agreement between the runtime and AST labellers ($\\kappa = 0.753$), was not met. A \\emph{phrasing cluster} is a connected component, within one idea, of programs whose AST 4-gram shingle sets, computed with normalised identifiers, have Jaccard similarity at least $\\theta$; identifiers are renamed in order of appearance, and comments, docstrings and constants are dropped. $\\theta = 0.8$ is primary, with 0.7 and 0.9 as sensitivity values. We call the number of phrasing clusters within an idea its \\emph{phrasings}. Diversity over ideas is the Hill number of order 1 (Hill-1), the exponential of the Shannon entropy of the idea distribution~\\citep{Hill1973}, computed among correct programs and rarefied to a depth of 25 programs. The \\emph{number of ideas at depth 25} is the expected count of distinct ideas among 25 correct programs drawn from a cell.\n\n\\subsection{Common random numbers}\n\\label{sec:crn}\n\nEvery comparison of decoding conditions samples by inverse transform sampling with common random numbers: each seed owns one stream of uniform variates, and every condition maps the same variates through its own next-token distribution. A difference between two conditions on one seed is therefore caused by the condition, not by a different draw. For a block of conditions, the \\emph{change count} of a task is the number of seeds whose algorithm label differs anywhere across the block; we bound its rate with the Clopper-Pearson interval~\\citep{Clopper1934}. Thinking-mode arms ran in vLLM with a seed set for each request, which couples conditions through shared Gumbel noise~\\citep{Ravfogel2024}.\n\nThe temperature block ran each of 20 seeds per task (spread over five prompt templates) at $T$ = 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3 with top-$p$ 1, and as sensitivity conditions with top-$k$ 10 at $T = 0.7$ and with min-$p$ 0.1 at $T = 2.0$.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-4/experiment-21}} The comparison intervention is a random activation push: activation addition with a random rather than a learned direction, akin to noise steering. We call it a \\emph{random task-state push}: one isotropic unit direction is added, during the prefill only, to the residual stream activations at the token positions that state the task (the \\emph{task specification states}) in blocks 12 to 23. Its size is set in multiples $\\alpha$ of the displacement that a ban prompt induces at the same positions. Six fixed directions were run at $\\alpha = 1$ and 2.\n\n\\subsection{Locating the forking token}\n\\label{sec:fork}\n\nPrograms of different algorithms often share their first tokens; we call this common prefix the \\emph{shared opening}. Following Forking Paths analysis~\\citep{Bigelow2024}, we sample base programs, resample continuations from their prefixes at increasing lengths, label every completed continuation, and detect a change point in the algorithm distribution with a preregistered Bayesian rule calibrated against permutation nulls. The change point is refined to a single token and confirmed by forcing each candidate token and sampling continuations from it. When the branch after a forking token is not pure, a second forking token is searched inside it. Below, \\emph{the fork} is short for the forking token. We define the \\emph{fork margin} as the teacher-forced gap in log probability, at the forking token, between the class of tokens that lead to the default algorithm and the best class that leads elsewhere, and report $H(A \\mid \\text{class})$, the entropy of the algorithm given the forking token's class.\n\n\\subsection{A composed temperature law}\n\\label{sec:law}\n\nLet $O_c$ be the $c$-th shared opening that precedes a forking token, and $w_T(O_c)$ the probability of sampling it at temperature $T$, the product of tempered teacher-forced token probabilities along it. Let $\\pi_T(t \\mid O_c)$ be the tempered next-token distribution at the fork, renormalised over the top 10 logits for top-$k$ 10, and $P(A \\mid t)$ the share of algorithm $A$ among $T = 1$ continuations forced from token $t$. We call the prediction\n\\begin{equation}\nP_T(A) = \\sum_c w_T(O_c)\\Big[\\sum_t \\pi_T(t \\mid O_c)\\, G(t, A) + r_T(c)\\, P(A \\mid \\mathrm{rest}_c)\\Big] + \\Big(1 - \\sum_c w_T(O_c)\\Big)\\, q_{\\mathrm{rest}}(A)\n\\label{eq:law}\n\\end{equation}\nthe \\emph{composed law}. Here $G(t, A) = P(A \\mid t)$ unless $t$ opens a second fork, in which case $G$ is the same mixture taken over the second fork's tokens. The term $r_T(c)$ is the tempered mass outside the top 20 tokens, and $q_{\\mathrm{rest}}$ is the composition of samples that leave the located openings. The prediction is averaged over five prompt templates and uses only teacher-forced logits and $T = 1$ conditionals, so it can be committed before any temperature sample is drawn.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-8/experiment-43}}\n\nFour rivals were committed with it: a flat law that keeps the $T = 1$ shares at every temperature; a rival we call share tempering, which raises the $T = 1$ shares to the power $1/T$ and renormalises; a single fork law without the second level; and the same law at the position of highest entropy instead of the located fork. Each predictor is scored by its mean absolute error (MAE), the mean over the four temperatures of the total variation distance between predicted and observed label distributions.\n\n\\subsection{Probing what sets the forking token}\n\\label{sec:probes}\n\n\\paragraph{Task-state exchange.} We call the following interchange intervention a \\emph{task-state exchange}. A forced prompt (\\texttt{Implement the task with $\\langle$minority algorithm$\\rangle$}) is paired with a \\emph{padding twin} in which the instruction is replaced by padding tokens so that all positions align. We write the task specification states of the forced prompt into the forward pass of the twin and sample on shared streams, against a random exchange matched in norm.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-7/experiment-35}}\n\n\\paragraph{Base against instruct.} Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-8B-Base are teacher-forced on identical token ids formatted with the chat template, at the forking tokens and at 64 phrasing positions of 20 programs per task. We compare fork margins, next-token entropies and Jensen--Shannon divergences, and count how often the token of the instruct model is the top token of the base model, following the URIAL token categories~\\citep{Lin2023}.\n\n\\subsection{Other controls and the novelty audit}\n\\label{sec:controls}\n\nTo bound the result we also measured random context seeds (\\code{seed=d32qxk4nt43} and \\code{seed=(horse chair roof love)} prepended to the prompt) and a \\emph{semantic seed}, a paragraph that implies an algorithm without naming it. We further measured instructions from \\code{be creative} to a 2,000-word request for a fully novel algorithm, and \\emph{bans}, instructions not to use a named algorithm, either of the default alone or of five algorithms at once (we call the latter a \\emph{ban of five names}). A \\emph{survivor} is a correct program whose algorithm is not banned. Finally, we ran an island-model program search in the manner of FunSearch~\\citep{RomeraParedes2023}, in which the model mutates programs and a fixed evaluator keeps the best ones across generations. Every correct program labelled outside its task's catalogue was compared with a corpus of known solutions (about 18,000 programs built from LeetCode, textbook and benchmark solutions), read by blind LLM judges gated on known controls, and read manually. Zero novel programs in $n$ correct ones is reported with the rule-of-three bound $3/n$.\n\n\\section{Experimental Setup}\n\\label{sec:setup}\n\n\\paragraph{Preregistration.} Every decisive prediction, threshold and analysis rule was written to a SHA-256 hash chain before the samples it governs were drawn, and each artifact's chain verifies end to end. The experiment with shared seeds preregistered four predictions: a temperature change count of at most 1 of 20 seeds in each of four cells (three tasks without thinking, shortest path with thinking); phrasings per idea that grow with temperature; a random push that changes at least 5 of 20 seeds on shortest path and on $k$-th smallest; and a positive contrast per seed between push and temperature, pooled over those two tasks, at one sided $p < 0.05$, which was the experiment's single entry in its secondary family of preregistered tests. The experiment is confirmed only if all four hold. The composed law's criterion was an MAE of at most 0.10 with $H(A \\mid \\text{class})$ at most 0.3 bits per unit, and passing on at least 70\\% of scored units including at least 3 held-out units, with at least 4 held-out units scored.\n\n\\paragraph{Units and samples.} The temperature block used 20 seeds per task and condition for Qwen3-8B on grid, shortest path and $k$-th smallest, run in an 8-bit engine whose rows reproduced the same cells of an earlier run token for token (200 of 200). The composed law was developed on trapped rain water, valid anagram and minimum spanning tree weight in Qwen3-8B and tested, before any Qwen3-8B sweep sample, on held-out units from two other families: substring search and first and last position in gemma-3-4b-it, and the grid task in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Each unit was swept on 100 fresh shared streams at $T$ = 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3 under top-$p$ 1 and top-$k$ 10, in bfloat16. Algorithm changes under activation pushes are not an artefact of the 8-bit engine: push directions move the algorithm about as often in bfloat16 as in the 8-bit engine (26 of 40 directions escape, by the criterion of Section~\\ref{sec:res-other}, on connected components against 29 in the 8-bit engine, and 6 against 8 on shortest path).\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-6/experiment-29}}\n\n\\paragraph{Statistics.} Paired binary contrasts use the exact McNemar test~\\citep{Mcnemar1947}; the contrast per seed between push and temperature uses a sign flip test, a permutation test that flips the sign of each seed's difference, with a bootstrap interval over seed slots; and proportions use Wilson or Clopper-Pearson intervals. Every headline number was rederived from raw rows by an independent script sharing no code with the analysis, and placebo versions of each test (shuffled conditions, shuffled temperature labels, shuffled token maps) were run and rejected at about their nominal rate. Code, prompts, raw generations, labels and the hash chains of every experiment are released with the paper, and each result below links to the code that produced it.\n\n\\section{Results}\n\\label{sec:results}\n\n\\subsection{A task-state push changes the algorithm where temperature does not}\n\\label{sec:res-push}\n\nOn the same random streams, a random task-state push, that is, one random direction added to the task specification states, changed the algorithm of Qwen3-8B in more seeds than temperature did, by a paired difference of 0.545 per seed (95\\% bootstrap CI 0.41 to 0.67), pooled over shortest path and $k$-th smallest (40 seeds; Figure~\\ref{fig:headline} and Table~\\ref{tab:seed}). For each seed, the contrast is the push's change indicator, averaged over the 20 subsets of three directions (each a union over its three directions at $\\alpha = 1$ and $T = 1.0$), minus the seed's change indicator across the four temperatures. It was the experiment's single entry in its secondary family of preregistered tests, and it held, with a one sided sign flip $p$ of $1.0\\times10^{-5}$. A permutation of conditions within each seed never reaches the observed mean (maximum placebo mean 0.155 in 200 permutations). The experiment as a whole is graded partial: its preregistered prediction that the push changes at least 5 of 20 seeds held on shortest path (17.25) but failed on $k$-th smallest (4.55). The contrast was run only in the 8-bit (W8A8) engine and was not rerun in bfloat16. The push itself does change the algorithm in bfloat16 at the same absolute push norm (Section~\\ref{sec:setup}).\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\caption{Seeds (of 20) whose algorithm changes across the conditions of a block, Qwen3-8B, same random stream per seed, 8-bit W8A8 engine except the thinking-mode arm (vLLM). Push rows, that is, rows for the random task-state push, are the mean over the 20 subsets of three of the six fixed directions of the number of seeds whose label differs anywhere among the unpushed arm and the three directions.}\n  \\label{tab:seed}\n  \\small\n  \\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{@{}L C{2.5cm} C{2.5cm} C{2.2cm}@{}}\n    \\toprule\n    Conditions on the same seeds & Shortest path (Dijkstra) & $k$-th smallest (full sort) & Grid path (BFS) \\\\\n    \\midrule\n    Temperature 0.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3, top-$p$ 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\\n    The same, plus top-$k$ 10 at $T$ 0.7 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\\n    The same, plus min-$p$ 0.1 at $T$ 2.0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\\\\n    Temperature 0.3 to 1.3, thinking mode & 0 & not run & 0 (of 10) \\\\\n    \\midrule\n    Random task-state push, $\\alpha = 1$, $T$ 1.0 & 17.25 & 4.55 & 2.50 \\\\\n    Random task-state push, $\\alpha = 2$, $T$ 1.0 & 19.05 & 10.60 & 8.70 \\\\\n    \\bottomrule\n  \\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nA single push direction at $\\alpha = 1$ changed 7, 10, 15, 17, 3 and 8 of 20 seeds on shortest path and up to 7 of 20 on $k$-th smallest. The algorithms the changed programs moved to, their \\emph{landings}, were Bellman-Ford/SPFA (52 of 60 programs off the default on shortest path) and quickselect (11 of 11 on $k$-th smallest). The push is not free: pass rates on shortest path fell from 1.00 to 0.63 at $\\alpha = 1$ and 0.42 at $\\alpha = 2$.\n\nTemperature, on the same seeds, never changed the algorithm on any of the three default tasks. Across $T$ = 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3, all 20 seeds kept their algorithm on shortest path (Dijkstra), on $k$-th smallest (full sort) and on the grid task (BFS). The change count is 0 of 20 per task, with an exact 95\\% upper bound of 0.168 on the change rate per seed. This was a separate preregistered prediction (at most 1 of 20 seeds per cell), and it held under every reading: counting only correct programs, counting invalid outputs as a label, and adding top-$k$ 10 as a fifth condition all leave the count at 0. Adding min-$p$ 0.1 at $T = 2.0$ changes one seed on shortest path and one on $k$-th smallest. With thinking mode enabled, shortest path kept Dijkstra in 20 of 20 seeds, every final program and every first approach named in the thinking trace was Dijkstra, and all 100 traces completed within the 16k-token cap. The reduced grid arm kept BFS in 10 of 10 seeds.\n\nPhrasings, in contrast, grow with temperature (Figure~\\ref{fig:phrasings}). On the grid task the number of phrasing clusters among 20 programs rose from 3 at $T = 0.3$ to 10, 12 and 13 at $T$ = 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3, while the number of distinct algorithms stayed at 1 on all three tasks at every temperature. The pooled slope of log phrasings per idea on temperature is 0.70 per unit $T$ (95\\% CI 0.35 to 0.93) at Jaccard threshold 0.8, and 0.64 [0.30, 0.89] and 0.81 [0.33, 0.98] at 0.7 and 0.9. Almost all of the growth comes from the grid task, while shortest path moves from 1 to 2 clusters and $k$-th smallest stays at 2.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig3_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Counts of phrasing clusters and of distinct algorithms across sampling temperature, under a shared random stream (Qwen3-8B, non-thinking mode, top-$p$ 1, 20 seeds per task, one program per seed and temperature; same seeds as Figure~\\ref{fig:headline} and Table~\\ref{tab:seed}). Solid lines with markers give phrasing clusters among the 20 programs drawn on the same seeds on each task -- blue circles for grid path (BFS), orange squares for shortest path (Dijkstra), green triangles for $k$-th smallest (full sort) -- where a cluster is a connected component of programs whose AST 4-gram Jaccard similarity, with identifiers normalised, is at least 0.8. The black dashed line with diamond markers gives distinct algorithms among the same programs, which is 1 on all three tasks at every temperature, as the annotation inside the figure states (algorithm changed in 0 of 20 seeds per task; exact 95\\% upper bound 0.168 on the change rate per seed). Phrasing diversity rises steeply with temperature on the grid path task (3 to 13 clusters) and stays close to flat on the other two (1 rising to 2 on shortest path; constant at 2 on $k$-th smallest), while the dashed line never leaves 1.}\n  \\label{fig:phrasings}\n\\end{figure}\n\nThe temperature null replicates outside the design with common random numbers and outside the 8-bit engine. With 100 independent samples per cell, 797 of 800 grid programs were BFS and 797 of 800 shortest path programs were Dijkstra across eight temperature and sampler cells in non-thinking mode, and 800 of 800 in thinking mode. Over the same cells, grid phrasing clusters at threshold 0.8 rose from 4 to 36 with top-$k$ 10 and from 3 to 24 with top-$p$ 0.95. The literal setting of thinking mode with top-$k$ 10 under one seed per stream again changed the shortest path algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds (one sided 95\\% upper bound 0.139),\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-5/experiment-27}} and in bfloat16, 100 samples at $T = 1.3$ from the forking position left the default unchanged on four tasks (Section~\\ref{sec:res-fork}). At tight temperature the model therefore writes one idea in a few phrasings, and loosening temperature multiplies the phrasings of that idea rather than adding ideas.\n\nWhich default a model writes depends on the model. Asked for a path search on a grid, Qwen3-8B writes BFS in 99 of 100 programs at $T = 1.0$ and Dijkstra in 100 of 100 on weighted shortest path. Gemma-3-4B writes DFS in 139 and BFS in 61 of 200 grid programs.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-6/experiment-31}} Llama-3.1-8B attempts BFS in 77 and DFS in 20 of 100, but its correct grid programs are all BFS.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-2/experiment-10}, \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-3/evaluation-2}}\n\n\\subsection{One or two forking tokens settle the algorithm}\n\\label{sec:res-fork}\n\nPrefix resampling places the decision at a single token after a shared opening on every unit where the instruct model writes two algorithms (Table~\\ref{tab:law}, fourth column). On minimum spanning tree weight the 61-token opening is followed by the word after the comment marker \\code{\\#}: \\tok{Kr} (probability 0.72) leads to Kruskal in every continuation, and \\tok{Prim} (0.27) to Prim in 97\\%. On trapped rain water, after \\code{if not height: return 0}, \\tok{n} leads to prefix and suffix arrays and \\tok{left} to two pointers. On valid anagram, after the length check, \\tok{return} leads to sorting and \\tok{count} to counting. Given the class of the located forking token, the remaining entropy of the algorithm, $H(A \\mid \\text{class})$, is 0.050 bits [95\\% CI 0.014, 0.096], 0.153 and 0.189 bits on these three units, against the preregistered limit of 0.3. A blind locator with a frozen change-point rule recovered the same tokens on fresh paths, where the remaining entropy was at most 0.004 bits on the five Qwen3-8B and Gemma units (Table~\\ref{tab:law}). The same structure appears in other tasks and families. Connected components in Qwen3-8B is settled at generated tokens 10 to 11, where a \\tok{parent} or \\code{def find} line leads to union find and \\code{def dfs} to graph search, with 0 bits left at token 11.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-7/experiment-34}} Gemma's grid prompt forks at response index 32: \\tok{visited} leads to DFS ($P(\\text{BFS}) = 0.011$), and a newline, \\code{if} or \\tok{queue} to BFS (0.95 to 1.00). Shortest path has no single forking token within its first 60 tokens.\n\nOn the default tasks the forking token is decided by a wide margin. At the located forking position, the teacher-forced fork margin of the default is 7.46 nats on the grid task, 4.85 on shortest path, 17.04 on connected components and 6.10 on $k$-th smallest. Averaged over five prompt templates instead, the margins on the first three tasks are 6.33, 5.61 and 15.96 nats (Figure~\\ref{fig:base}). Dividing these logits by 1.3 predicts at most 0.02 of samples off the default at $T = 1.3$, and 100 samples at $T = 1.3$ from the forking position produced no program off the default on any of the four tasks. A further 20 samples gave one program off the default on each of the grid and shortest path tasks. The temperature null of Section~\\ref{sec:res-push} is what these margins predict: a temperature of 1.3 scales a 5 to 17 nat gap by $1/1.3$ and leaves the alternative out of reach.\n\n\\subsection{The forking-token logits predict the temperature response}\n\\label{sec:res-law}\n\nWhere the forking token is contested, the composed law predicts how temperature moves the algorithm mix (Table~\\ref{tab:law} and Figure~\\ref{fig:law}). The law was committed before any temperature sample and scored on 100 fresh shared streams per cell. It passed its unit criterion on five of six units: the three development units in Qwen3-8B (MAE 0.029, 0.054 and 0.043) and both held-out Gemma units (0.033 on substring search and 0.014 on first and last position). On first and last position the first forking token is impure, and the second level found inside it lowers the error from 0.051 for the single fork law to 0.014 (bootstrap 95\\% CI of the difference $-0.051$ to $-0.011$). Lowering temperature from 1.0 to 0.3 removed the minority in one direction only on both Gemma units (10:0 and 13:0 discordant streams, McNemar $p = 0.001$ and $1.2\\times10^{-4}$) and on minimum spanning tree weight (18:0, $p = 3.8\\times10^{-6}$).\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\caption{The composed temperature law against its four rivals: mean absolute error (mean total variation distance over $T$ = 0.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3; 100 shared streams per cell). Development units were used to build the law; held-out units were committed and swept before any sweep of a development unit. Lowest error per row in bold. The built-in index, that is, a call to the language's own string search instead of an implemented algorithm, is the minority algorithm on substring search.}\n  \\label{tab:law}\n  \\footnotesize\n  \\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{2.6pt}\n  \\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{@{}L C{0.7cm} R{1.5cm} R{1.4cm} C{1.35cm} C{0.8cm} C{1.38cm} C{0.95cm} C{1.25cm} C{1.25cm} C{0.6cm}@{}}\n    \\toprule\n    Unit (model) & Held out & Minority algorithm & Forking token(s) & Composed law & Flat & Share tempering & Single fork & Highest entropy position & $H(A \\mid \\text{class})$, bits & Pass \\\\\n    \\midrule\n    Trapped rain water (Qwen3-8B) & no & Two pointers & 18 and 19 & \\textbf{0.029} & 0.055 & 0.070 & 0.038 & 0.037 & $<0.001$ & yes \\\\\n    Valid anagram (Qwen3-8B) & no & Fixed count array & 24 and 26 & 0.054 & \\textbf{0.030} & 0.091 & 0.054 & 0.071 & $<0.001$ & yes \\\\\n    Minimum spanning tree weight (Qwen3-8B) & no & Prim & 61 & \\textbf{0.043} & 0.093 & 0.058 & \\textbf{0.043} & 0.045 & 0.004 & yes \\\\\n    Substring search (Gemma-3-4B) & yes & Built-in index & 31 & 0.033 & 0.043 & \\textbf{0.023} & 0.033 & 0.036 & 0.001 & yes \\\\\n    First and last position (Gemma-3-4B) & yes & Binary search & 12 and 24 & \\textbf{0.014} & 0.073 & 0.018 & 0.051 & 0.017 & 0.001 & yes \\\\\n    Grid path (Llama-3.1-8B) & yes & DFS & after a 52-token opening & 0.142 & 0.138 & 0.143 & 0.142 & \\textbf{0.134} & 0.63 & no \\\\\n    \\bottomrule\n  \\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nThe preregistered claim is graded partial. Five of six scored units pass (0.83, above the 0.70 bar), but only three held-out units were scored where the claim required four, so the held-out criterion is underpowered rather than met. No held-out unit exceeded the disconfirming error of 0.2. The law is also not clearly better than simpler rivals. It has the lowest error on three of six units and beats the flat law on four of six (exact sign test $p = 0.34$). Bootstrap intervals of the difference, resampling streams, exclude 0 on minimum spanning tree weight [$-0.050$, $-0.025$], first and last position [$-0.081$, $-0.018$] and substring search [$-0.041$, $-0.002$]. Share tempering beats it on substring search, and the flat law beats it on valid anagram, where temperature barely moves the mix. The law adds most where an impure first fork needs the second level and where the minority is not simply sharpened away.\n\nOn the grid task of Llama-3.1-8B every predictor fails. Llama reaches the forking tokens through many openings, so the two confirmed openings cover about 2\\% of samples and the committed law is almost the flat law. At $T = 1.3$, 72 of 100 programs run to the token cap and the pass rate falls to 0.04, a collapse into unusable code that no law over algorithm shares predicts. An earlier, smaller test of the single fork law on 50 streams per cell passed on one of three Qwen3-8B units. Replaying each stream's own uniforms through the committed token classes reproduced the observed shares there (0.08, 0.18, 0.18 and 0.16 against 0.10, 0.18, 0.18 and 0.20 on trapped rain water), locating the misses in the finite sample rather than in the mechanism.\n\nApplying temperature only at the forking token tests the account causally. With the dose committed from teacher-forced logits, predicted algorithm shares matched the observed ones with MAE 0.010 to 0.047 on five located units, and Hill-1 among correct programs on valid anagram rose from 1.78 to 2.78 at a cost of 2 percentage points of pass rate.\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-8/experiment-39}} On connected components, a default task, the same treatment reached DFS in only 3 and 9 of 50 programs, and the larger dose cost 14 percentage points of pass rate because the alternative tokens at the fork break the format.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig4_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Predicted and observed share of the minority algorithm at four sampling temperatures (0.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3; top-$p$ = 1, $N$ = 100 generations per cell, shared random streams across temperatures), for six algorithm-choice units: three Qwen3-8B development units -- (a) trapped rain water: two pointers, (b) valid anagram: fixed count array, (c) minimum spanning tree weight: Prim -- and three held-out units -- (d) Gemma-3-4B substring search: built-in index, that is, a call to the language's own string search, (e) Gemma-3-4B first/last position: binary search, (f) Llama-3.1-8B grid path: DFS. Black circles give the observed minority share with vertical Wilson 95\\% confidence intervals; the solid blue line with small markers is the composed forking-token law's prediction, fixed before any temperature sample; the dashed grey line is the flat law, a reference that holds the $T$ = 1 share constant across temperature. Each panel title gives the mean absolute error, over the four temperature points, of the composed law and the flat law respectively. The algorithm a code model writes behaves like an almost discrete decision taken at one or two tokens early in the program, and temperature acts on that decision only through the next-token distribution there; a push of the task specification states acts upstream, on the states that set that distribution (Section~\\ref{sec:res-sets}). This single account explains the three regimes we observed. Where post-training has widened the fork margin to 4.85 to 17.04 nats, a temperature of 1.3 cannot reach the alternative, so the algorithm is fixed while every other position, where the next token is less certain, varies more. That is the phrasing growth of Figure~\\ref{fig:phrasings}. Where the forking token is contested, temperature sharpens or flattens the same two or three known algorithms at the rate the forking-token logits predict. And where the model reaches the decision through many openings, as Llama does on the grid task, the choice is spread over the opening and no law at a single token captures it. In the terms of the question that motivates this work, a tight temperature with top-$k$ 10 gives one idea in a few phrasings, and a loose one gives the same idea, or the same few ideas, in more phrasings.\n\nThis account reconciles two findings that look contradictory. \\citet{Lee2025} report that temperature above 1 raises algorithmic diversity among correct programs, and we find that temperature never changes the algorithm on default tasks. Both hold. On tasks whose fork is contested, temperature moves mass between known algorithms at the predicted rate; Prim on minimum spanning tree weight rises from 0.07 at $T = 0.3$ to 0.31 at $T = 1.3$. On tasks whose fork is decided by several nats, it does not. A diversity evaluation that pools tasks will see an average of the two. Our results also bear on the claim that a model returns the average answer and that only context moves it elsewhere. The instruct default is not the base model's average: post-training moved and sharpened one token, often promoting the base model's second or third choice, and left the repertoire unchanged.\n\nFor practice, the account says where to spend randomness. Temperature is a poor exploration control for algorithm choice, and on contested units its effect can be predicted before sampling from the forking-token logits. Controls that act upstream of the fork, such as context that implies an algorithm, a prompt that lists approaches and then picks one, or perturbations of the task specification states, do change the algorithm, but they move it to the second choice the model already knows, and at a cost in correctness. The audits found no route from any control applied to single samples to a correct novel algorithm. An evaluator that keeps improvements across generations made the same 8B model better than the textbook rule on bin packing, which is where the field's discovery systems operate~\\citep{RomeraParedes2023,Novikov2025}. Whether it made the model new remains open after the replication found none.\n\nFor interpretability, the results suggest that readouts of a plan taken before the code starts should be validated against the forking token. Natural language and sparse-feature readouts found no verbalised plan before the code, and fitted subspace edits at the fork moved the algorithm without passing the controls that would make them a variable of the model, consistent with the interpretability illusions that subspace patching can produce~\\citep{Makelov2023}. The forking token is where intervention is cheap and measurable, but a certified mechanism for the choice is still missing.\n\n\\section{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\nThe headline contrast between the push and temperature ran only in an 8-bit (W8A8) engine and was not rerun in bfloat16; the push alone changes the algorithm in bfloat16 at the same absolute push norm, but the paired contrast was not repeated, and it pools two tasks, with the grid task moving only 2.50 of 20 seeds. Most results come from one model, Qwen3-8B, in non-thinking mode. The composed law was tested on three held-out units in two other families; two passed and Llama's grid task failed, below the four held-out units the preregistered claim required, so the law's generality is an open question. The law was also not clearly better than the flat law, a baseline that predicts no change (four of six units, sign test $p = 0.34$), which means that much of its accuracy reflects how little temperature moves these units. The temperature null on shared seeds rests on 20 seeds per task, which bounds the change rate per seed below 0.17 per task, not at zero, and it ran with 8-bit linear layers; the bfloat16 fork margins and the grid sweep with independent samples agree with it, but the thinking-mode evidence is limited to shortest path and a 10-seed grid arm.\n\nThe tasks are short, well-known programming problems whose solutions are likely memorised, with catalogues of three to ten known algorithms; the conclusions may not hold for open-ended programs or for problems without a textbook solution. Experiments ran on different engines (bfloat16 and 8-bit linear layers, vLLM and Hugging Face); push escapes reproduced in bfloat16, but pushed cells showed precision sensitivity at the level of single streams. Phrasing clusters depend on a Jaccard threshold over AST shingles with normalised identifiers, and the growth was driven mostly by the grid task.\n\nLabels and the novelty audit carry their own uncertainty. Labellers were gated per task, but the gate failed by its strict criteria for the decoding experiment with independent samples and for the agreement between runtime and AST labels on the path tasks ($\\kappa = 0.753$), and the expansion-order tracer used for the ban of five names failed its gold gate, so those numbers are descriptive. In the program search no LLM judge passed its control gate, so novelty there rests on manual reads, and one reader's eight candidates were not reproduced by the replication. The geometry in activation space is correlational, and the map built from names is confounded by lexical overlap between algorithm names.\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\\label{sec:conclusion}\n\nOn the same random streams, a random push of Qwen3-8B's task specification states changed the algorithm in more seeds than temperature did, by 0.545 per seed (95\\% CI 0.41 to 0.67) over shortest path and $k$-th smallest, a preregistered contrast that held in an 8-bit engine and is untested in bfloat16. Temperature from 0.3 to 1.3 left the default algorithm unchanged in all 60 seeds (20 per task) while phrasings multiplied, because a forking token, not temperature, chooses the algorithm. Fork margins of 4.85 to 17.04 nats on the default tasks, widened by post-training, account for the null, and on contested forks the forking-token logits committed before sampling predicted the temperature response within 0.014 to 0.054 total variation on five of six units. No control we tested produced a correct algorithm outside the known repertoire.\n\nFuture work follows directly:\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item testing the composed law on more held-out units and families, including models that reach the fork through many openings;\n  \\item extending the forking-token analysis to thinking traces, where the first approach named was fixed in every trace we read;\n  \\item spending sampling randomness at forking tokens inside program search, and measuring whether it buys ideas rather than phrasings;\n  \\item searching for a variable of the algorithm choice that passes controls with permuted labels and with randomly initialised networks.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\section*{Code and Data Availability}\n\nCode, prompts, raw generations, algorithm labels and the preregistration hash chains of every experiment are public at \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract}; the footnotes in Sections~\\ref{sec:intro} to~\\ref{sec:results} link each result to the code that produced it.\n\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n\\bibliography{references}\n\n\\end{document}\n", "numLines": 110, "startLine": 249, "totalLines": 358}}

<main id="main" tabindex="-1">

<header class="hero">
<h1>A Random Activation Push Changes a Code Model's Algorithm Where Temperature Does Not</h1>
<div class="hero-grid">
<div class="tldr">
<p class="tldr-label">TL;DR</p>
<p class="tldr-text">Sampling temperature is often treated as the creativity control of a language model. This paper asks whether it changes <em>which algorithm</em> a code model implements, or only how the model writes the same one. With the random draws held fixed per seed, temperature from 0.3 to 1.3 never changed the algorithm Qwen3-8B wrote, in 20 seeds on each of three tasks, while the number of phrasings grew. A random push to the model's internal states at the prompt tokens that state the task did change it, in more seeds than temperature did: a paired difference of <strong>0.545 per seed</strong> (95% CI 0.41 to 0.67), pooled over shortest path and <var>k</var>-th smallest. The algorithm is settled at one or two forking tokens early in the program, where the default leads by several nats, more than this temperature range can overcome.</p>
</div>
<aside class="headline" aria-label="Headline number">
<p class="headline-num">0.545</p>
<p class="headline-label">seeds changed per seed: random task-state push minus temperature, on the same random streams</p>
<p class="headline-meta">95% CI 0.41 to 0.67; one-sided sign-flip <var>p</var> = 1.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. Qwen3-8B, shortest path and <var>k</var>-th smallest, 40 seeds.</p>
<p class="headline-meta">A preregistered contrast that held, in an experiment graded partial. It ran only in an 8-bit (W8A8) engine and is untested in bfloat16.</p>
</aside>
</div>
<div class="hero-links">
<ul class="doc-links">
<li><a class="btn btn-primary" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract@fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/paper.pdf">Read the paper (PDF)</a></li>
<li><a class="btn" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract@fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/report.pdf">Read the full research report</a></li>

<li><a class="btn" href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC">Code repository</a></li>
</ul>
<p class="rounds"><span class="rounds-label">Round reports:</span> <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract@fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-1/report.pdf">Round 1</a> <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract@fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-2/report.pdf">Round 2</a> <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract@fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-3/report.pdf">Round 3</a> <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract@fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-4/report.pdf">Round 4</a> <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract@fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-5/report.pdf">Round 5</a> <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract@fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-6/report.pdf">Round 6</a> <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract@fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-7/report.pdf">Round 7</a> <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract@fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-8/report.pdf">Round 8</a> <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract@fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-9/report.pdf">Round 9</a> <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract@fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-10/report.pdf">Round 10</a></p>
</div>

<section id="contributions" class="section" aria-labelledby="contributions-h">
<h2 id="contributions-h">Contributions</h2>
<ol class="cards">
<li class="card">
<h3>A task-state push changes the algorithm where temperature does not</h3>
<p>On the same random streams, a random push to the task specification states changed the algorithm in more seeds than temperature did, by 0.545 per seed (95% CI 0.41 to 0.67) over shortest path and <var>k</var>-th smallest. Temperature from 0.3 to 1.3 changed it in 0 of 20 seeds on each of three tasks, while phrasing clusters on the grid task rose from 3 to 13.</p>
</li>
<li class="card">
<h3>One or two forking tokens settle the algorithm</h3>
<p>Given the class of the forking token, at most 0.19 bits of uncertainty about the algorithm remain. On four default tasks the default leads at that token by a fork margin of 4.85 to 17.04 nats.</p>
</li>
<li class="card">
<h3>A law built from that token's logits predicts temperature's effect</h3>
<p>Committed before sampling, it matched the observed algorithm mix across four temperatures within a mean total variation distance of 0.014 to 0.054 on five of six units, two of them held-out Gemma-3-4B units. It failed on Llama-3.1-8B's grid task (0.142), and a baseline that predicts no change was close.</p>
</li>
<li class="card">
<h3>Task states and post-training set the fork</h3>
<p>Writing the task specification states of a prompt that names the minority algorithm into an aligned copy without that instruction produced the minority algorithm in 30 of 30 samples on each of three tasks. On the three default tasks, post-training widened fork margins by 2.11 to 13.41 nats while changing entropy at phrasing positions by less than 0.5 nats.</p>
</li>
<li class="card">
<h3>Other controls reweight the same repertoire</h3>
<p>Random seeds, novelty instructions, bans, activation pushes and program search moved programs among known algorithms. No audit found a correct novel algorithm, and where a ban of five names lands in activation space depends on whether the map is built from names or from programs.</p>
</li>
</ol>
</section>

<section id="method" class="section" aria-labelledby="method-h">
<h2 id="method-h">Method</h2>
<figure class="fig">
<div class="fig-scroll"><a class="zoom mw-800" href="figures/fig2_v0.jpg" data-open-figure="1" aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-label="Enlarge Figure 2: Where the algorithm is decided"><img src="figures/fig2_v0.jpg" width="3819" height="1043" alt="Diagram of the account: a prompt asking for the total weight of a minimum spanning tree feeds a shared 61-token code opening, then a forking token where the token Kr, at probability 0.72, leads to Kruskal and the token Prim, at 0.27, leads to Prim, each written in many phrasings. Arrows mark the task-state exchange and the random task-state push entering at the prompt's task-specification states, and a thermometer marks temperature acting only at the fork."></a></div>
<p class="fig-hint">Scroll the figure sideways, or select it to enlarge.</p>
<figcaption><strong>Figure 2. Where the algorithm is decided.</strong> Schematic illustration of the account and of the measurements (not data), using one minimum spanning tree example. <a href="#fig-2">Full caption in the gallery</a>.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p class="lede">The method has one aim: to tell a change of algorithm apart from a change of wording, and to find the token at which the algorithm is chosen.</p>

<h3>What goes in</h3>
<p>Coding prompts whose possible answers are known in advance. The study starts from two path search tasks. In the grid task, <code>solve(grid, start, goal)</code> returns a valid path on a grid with walls; its catalogue holds breadth-first search (BFS), depth-first search (DFS), bidirectional BFS, iterative deepening DFS, A* and unit weight Dijkstra. The weighted shortest path task works on a directed graph, with a catalogue of Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford with its queue variant SPFA, bidirectional Dijkstra, Floyd-Warshall and Dial's algorithm. Each has 40 to 48 seeded hidden test cases with a time limit per case, and reference implementations of every catalogue algorithm that pass all tests.<a class="src" href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-1/experiment-1">code<span class="vh">: Where an algorithm ban sends an AI coder</span></a> A further 13 tasks, the bench, were derived from LeetCode problems with frozen wording and catalogues of 3 to 6 algorithms each, 684 hidden test cases in total, and references for all 54 catalogue algorithms.<a class="src" href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-2/experiment-11">code<span class="vh">: Coding-task bench with a baseline pilot</span></a></p>
<p>The main model is Qwen3-8B, in non-thinking mode unless stated, with Qwen3-8B-Base for the post-training comparison. Held-out units come from Gemma-3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with thinking enter the ban experiments. A <em>unit</em> is a task paired with one model. It is a <em>default task</em> when the instruct model writes one algorithm in essentially all samples, and a <em>mixed unit</em> when its unperturbed samples already contain a second algorithm at a share of roughly 0.1 to 0.4.</p>

<h3>What happens to it</h3>
<ol class="steps">
<li><p><strong>Each program is labelled by what it does when run.</strong> A sandboxed runtime tracer records queue, stack and heap operations, edge relaxations and grid reads; it is combined with AST rules, and a blind LLM judge breaks disagreements. On the bench tasks the runtime and AST labellers agreed at Cohen's κ 0.84 to 1.00. On the path tasks the combined label agreed with an adjudicated gold label at κ = 0.966, with 22 of 22 references correct, though the stricter criterion of that gate (κ = 0.753 between the runtime and AST labellers) was not met. A program is correct when it passes every hidden test.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Ideas are counted apart from phrasings.</strong> The runtime label of a correct program is its <em>idea</em>. Within one idea, programs whose AST 4-gram shingle sets, with identifiers normalised, have Jaccard similarity of at least 0.8 form one <em>phrasing cluster</em>; 0.7 and 0.9 serve as sensitivity values. Diversity over ideas is the Hill number of order 1 (Hill-1) among correct programs.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Conditions share one random stream per seed.</strong> Each seed owns one stream of uniform variates, and every condition maps the same variates through its own next-token distribution, so a difference on one seed is caused by the condition, not by a different draw. A task's <em>change count</em> is the number of seeds whose algorithm label differs anywhere across a block of conditions. The temperature block ran 20 seeds per task, spread over five prompt templates, at <var>T</var> = 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3 with top-<var>p</var> 1, plus top-<var>k</var> 10 at <var>T</var> = 0.7 and min-<var>p</var> 0.1 at <var>T</var> = 2.0 as sensitivity conditions.<a class="src" href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-4/experiment-21">code<span class="vh">: Same seed: temperature vs plan nudges</span></a></p></li>
<li><p><strong>A random push enters at the task states.</strong> One isotropic unit direction is added, during the prefill only, to the residual stream activations at the prompt tokens that state the task (the <em>task specification states</em>) in blocks 12 to 23. Its size is a multiple α of the displacement that a ban prompt induces at the same positions. Six fixed directions were run at α = 1 and 2.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Prefix resampling finds the forking token.</strong> Following Forking Paths analysis, base programs are resampled from their prefixes at increasing lengths, every continuation is labelled, and a preregistered Bayesian change-point rule, calibrated against permutation nulls, detects where the algorithm distribution shifts. The change point is refined to a single token and confirmed by forcing each candidate. The <em>fork margin</em> is the teacher-forced gap in log probability, at that token, between the class of tokens that lead to the default algorithm and the best class that leads elsewhere.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>A law composed at the fork predicts temperature.</strong> It tempers the probability of each shared opening and of each token at the fork, and mixes the algorithm shares that follow each token at <var>T</var> = 1:</p>
<div class="eq-wrap" role="group" aria-label="The composed temperature law"><p class="eq"><var>P</var><sub><var>T</var></sub>(<var>A</var>) = ∑<sub><var>c</var></sub> <var>w</var><sub><var>T</var></sub>(<var>O</var><sub><var>c</var></sub>) [ ∑<sub><var>t</var></sub> <var>π</var><sub><var>T</var></sub>(<var>t</var> | <var>O</var><sub><var>c</var></sub>) <var>G</var>(<var>t</var>, <var>A</var>) + <var>r</var><sub><var>T</var></sub>(<var>c</var>) <var>P</var>(<var>A</var> | rest<sub><var>c</var></sub>) ] + (1 − ∑<sub><var>c</var></sub> <var>w</var><sub><var>T</var></sub>(<var>O</var><sub><var>c</var></sub>)) <var>q</var><sub>rest</sub>(<var>A</var>)</p></div>
<dl class="terms">
<dt><var>O</var><sub><var>c</var></sub>, <var>w</var><sub><var>T</var></sub>(<var>O</var><sub><var>c</var></sub>)</dt><dd>the <var>c</var>-th shared opening before a forking token, and the probability of sampling it at temperature <var>T</var>: the product of tempered teacher-forced token probabilities along it</dd>
<dt><var>π</var><sub><var>T</var></sub>(<var>t</var> | <var>O</var><sub><var>c</var></sub>)</dt><dd>the tempered next-token distribution at the fork, renormalised over the top 10 logits for top-<var>k</var> 10</dd>
<dt><var>G</var>(<var>t</var>, <var>A</var>)</dt><dd><var>P</var>(<var>A</var> | <var>t</var>), the share of algorithm <var>A</var> among <var>T</var> = 1 continuations forced from token <var>t</var>, or the same mixture over a second fork's tokens when <var>t</var> opens one</dd>
<dt><var>r</var><sub><var>T</var></sub>(<var>c</var>), <var>q</var><sub>rest</sub></dt><dd>the tempered mass outside the top 20 tokens, and the composition of samples that leave the located openings</dd>
</dl>
<p>The prediction is averaged over five prompt templates and uses only teacher-forced logits and <var>T</var> = 1 conditionals, so it can be committed before any temperature sample is drawn.<a class="src" href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-8/experiment-43">code<span class="vh">: Predicting how temperature shifts code ideas</span></a> Four rivals were committed with it: a flat law that keeps the <var>T</var> = 1 shares at every temperature; share tempering, which raises the <var>T</var> = 1 shares to the power 1/<var>T</var> and renormalises; a single fork law without the second level; and the same law at the position of highest entropy. Each is scored by its mean absolute error (MAE), the mean over the four temperatures of the total variation distance between predicted and observed label distributions.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Exchanges of internal states ask what sets the fork.</strong> A task-state exchange pairs a forced prompt (<code>Implement the task with ⟨minority algorithm⟩</code>) with a <em>padding twin</em> whose instruction is replaced by padding tokens, so that all positions align. The task specification states of the forced prompt are written into the forward pass of the twin, which then samples on shared streams, against a random exchange matched in norm.<a class="src" href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-7/experiment-35">code<span class="vh">: Where temperature changes the algorithm an LLM writes</span></a> Separately, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-8B-Base are teacher-forced on identical token ids, formatted with the chat template, at the forking tokens and at 64 phrasing positions of 20 programs per task.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Other controls and a novelty audit bound the result.</strong> Random context seeds (<code>seed=d32qxk4nt43</code> and <code>seed=(horse chair roof love)</code> prepended to the prompt), a semantic seed that implies an algorithm without naming it, instructions from <code>be creative</code> to a 2,000-word request for a fully novel algorithm, bans of one or of five algorithm names, and an island-model program search in the manner of FunSearch. Every correct program labelled outside its task's catalogue was compared with a corpus of about 18,000 known solutions, read by blind LLM judges gated on known controls, and read manually.</p></li>
</ol>

<h3>What comes out</h3>
<ul class="out-list">
<li>For each block of conditions, the change count per task, with its rate bounded by a Clopper-Pearson interval.</li>
<li>Phrasing clusters per idea, and the number of ideas at depth 25: the expected count of distinct ideas among 25 correct programs drawn from a cell.</li>
<li>The forking token of each unit, its fork margin in nats, and <var>H</var>(<var>A</var> | class), the entropy of the algorithm given the class of the forking token.</li>
<li>A committed prediction of the algorithm mix at each temperature, scored on 100 fresh shared streams per cell.</li>
<li>A count of correct novel algorithms, reported with the rule-of-three bound 3/<var>n</var> when it is zero.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Why it is built this way</h3>
<p>Counting distinct outputs cannot answer the question. Two programs can differ in every line and implement the same algorithm, and a program can name one algorithm while executing another, so labels come from what the code does when run. Comparisons across temperatures drawn with independent random numbers mix the effect of temperature with sampling noise: with a default share near 1.0, a few stray samples look like a temperature effect. Knowing that an algorithm changes also says nothing about where the decision was made. Prefix resampling answers that.</p>
<p>Every decisive prediction, threshold and analysis rule was written to a SHA-256 hash chain before the samples it governs were drawn. Every headline number was rederived from raw rows by an independent script sharing no code with the analysis, and placebo versions of each test were run and rejected at about their nominal rate.</p>
</section>

<section class="result" id="r-push" aria-labelledby="r-push-h">
<h3 id="r-push-h">A task-state push changes the algorithm where temperature does not</h3>
<div class="result-head">
<p class="stat"><span class="stat-num">0.545</span><span class="stat-unit">per seed</span><span class="stat-label">Paired difference in seeds changed, push (α = 1, <var>T</var> = 1.0) minus temperature. 95% bootstrap CI 0.41 to 0.67; one-sided sign-flip <var>p</var> = 1.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup>.</span></p>
<dl class="facts">
<div><dt>Measured on</dt><dd>Qwen3-8B, shortest path and <var>k</var>-th smallest pooled (40 seeds), one shared random stream per seed, 8-bit (W8A8) engine.</dd></div>
<div><dt>Compared against</dt><dd>Temperature 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3 on the same seeds. A permutation of conditions within each seed never reaches the observed mean (maximum placebo mean 0.155 in 200 permutations).</dd></div>
</dl>
</div>
<p>For each seed, the contrast is the push's change indicator, averaged over the 20 subsets of three directions, minus the seed's change indicator across the four temperatures. It was the experiment's single entry in its secondary family of preregistered tests, and it held. The experiment as a whole is graded partial: its prediction that the push changes at least 5 of 20 seeds held on shortest path (17.25) but failed on <var>k</var>-th smallest (4.55). The contrast was run only in the 8-bit engine and was not rerun in bfloat16.</p>
<p>The push itself does change the algorithm in bfloat16 at the same absolute push norm: 26 of 40 directions escape on connected components against 29 in the 8-bit engine, and 6 against 8 on shortest path.<a class="src" href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract/tree/fork/run_jSassd-YWLVC/round-6/experiment-29">code<span class="vh">: Is FP8 rounding behind the random-push escapes?</span></a> A single push direction at α = 1 changed 7, 10, 15, 17, 3 and 8 of 20 seeds on shortest path and up to 7 of 20 on <var>k</var>-th smallest. The changed programs landed on Bellman-Ford/SPFA (52 of 60 programs off the default on shortest path) and quickselect (11 of 11 on <var>k</var>-th smallest). The push is not free. Pass rates on shortest path fell from 1.00 to 0.63 at α = 1 and 0.42 at α = 2.</p>
